\paragraph{Classification vs.\ Generation in NLP.}
The question of how task framing affects model performance has a rich history in NLP.
T5~\cite{raffel2020t5} demonstrates that casting diverse tasks into a unified text-to-text format achieves strong performance but also reveals that task framing choices affect results under controlled capacity.
BART~\cite{lewis2020bart} shows generation--classification tradeoffs across NLP tasks, with extractive approaches sometimes outperforming generative ones.
SQuAD~\cite{rajpurkar2016squad} frames question answering as span extraction---constraining the output space---rather than open-ended generation, simplifying the task without sacrificing answer quality.
We extend this lens to code verification, identifying \emph{code complexity} as the key moderator: classification and generation converge on simple code but diverge sharply as complexity grows, with the transition point marking where generation failure modes become dominant.

tool_args.old_string: Two dominant paradigms have emerged for execution-free verification, each with distinct trade-offs. \textbf{Generation-based simulation}~\cite{meta2025cwm,maimon2026selfexecution}: Code World Models predict the execution output string for each test, then derive pass/fail verdicts by exact match against expected outputs. This approach works well when outputs are short and structurally simple, but suffers from three systematic failure modes as complexity increases. First, \emph{token-budget exhaustion}: when the true output length exceeds the generation budget, the predicted string is truncated, producing a spurious failure verdict regardless of model capability. Second, \emph{string-value prediction errors}: complex return types---floating-point numbers, nested dictionaries, sets with arbitrary ordering---require exact string reproduction, and minor formatting differences cause false rejections even when the model has correctly inferred the semantic output. Third, \emph{format compliance collapse}: at repository-level complexity, the model fails to produce outputs in the required structured format altogether---the majority of \cwm{} predictions become unparseable, and among the parseable remainder, accuracy drops to 42--43\%, below chance level (50\%).

tool_args.old_string: \textbf{Trajectory-level scoring}~\cite{shum2025swerm} takes the opposite approach: a reward model predicts binary patch-level correctness from the full code context, bypassing generation entirely.
